To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the composition of two segrass species in a lagoon was not affected over a period of more than 17 years, but the abundance of each species varied.
seagrass composition did not vary in a lagoon, but their relative abundances and fine structures did.

spatial and temporal variations of seagrass species in a lagoon were affected by their relative abundances and fine structures, and that these variations in turn affected the habitat quality of motile epifaunal animals, especially a commercial shrimp.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the importance of considering the fine structures of seagrass species when assessing the habitat quality for motiles, especially commercially exploited species.
the spatial and temporal variations of seagrass species and how those changes affected the habitat quality for motility animals, especially for a commercially exploited shrimp.
the effects of the distribution dynamics of two seagrasses on the abundance of commercially important shrimp.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the seagrass community structure is not static, but rather varies in space and time and that the variations affect the habitat quality for commercially exploited species.
seagrass distribution is a dynamic process that changes with the seasons.
the spatial and temporal dynamics of seagrasses are important in the management of commercially exploited species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spatial and temporal changes in the seagrass distribution and their fine structure are important for the management of commercially exploited motile epifaunal species.
the seagrass bed in this lagoon is a habitat that can be used by a wide variety of animals and that its quality is affected by the species composition, abundance, and fine structures of seagrasses.
seagrass beds are dynamic ecosystems and their dynamics should be considered for the management of seagrass resources and their associated fauna.
The main takeaway from our work is that
seagrass beds can be managed to maintain habitat quality for commercial species.
the management of a commercially harvested species should consider not only the abundance of the species but also the composition of the habitat.

seagrasses with similar aboveground morphologies have different belowground morphologies and that these differences can be important for understanding the ecology and management of associated organisms, especially commercially exploited species.
